title: Where It Thinks It Is: Odometry, and Which Error Costs What

questions.question: A robot's odometry is perfect at startup and poor an hour later, and restarting fixes it. What is happening?
options: Every error that enters the estimate stays in, because nothing ever corrects it
A counter is overflowing
The encoders are degrading as they warm up
Memory is leaking into the pose
questions.explanation: That is not a defect to fix, it is what dead reckoning is. The defect is treating an estimate whose error grows as though it were a measurement whose error does not.

questions.question: A wheel base that is one percent wrong costs how much over a hundred metres driven straight?
options: Nothing at all, because the base only ever divides the difference between the wheels
One metre, the same as any one percent error
About 1.75 metres
It depends on the wheel radius
questions.explanation: Driving straight that difference is zero. Drive the same distance with turns in it and the same error costs over a metre, which is why a straight line calibration says nothing about the wheel base.

questions.question: A heading that starts one degree wrong costs 1.75 m over a straight hundred metres and 0.11 m around a closed square. Why the difference?
options: On a straight run the offset is distance times its tangent and grows; around a loop it largely cancels on the way back
The square is shorter
Turning corrects the heading
The measurement is noisier on the square
questions.explanation: Which is the mirror image of the wheel base result, and together they are the reason to calibrate each parameter on the path that exposes it.

questions.question: Why does the position step use the heading held at the start of the step?
options: Either convention is a straight line where the robot drove an arc, and the point is to pick one and integrate often
The new heading would be undefined
It is required for the wrap to work
Using the new heading doubles the turn
questions.explanation: Measured on a quarter circle, the error is close to the length of one step and halves when the step does, which is an argument for updating often rather than for a cleverer formula.

questions.question: What is the most useful thing to report alongside a dead reckoned pose?
options: How far it has driven since the last correction, since the error grows with distance rather than with the clock
The time since startup
The number of encoder ticks
The current wheel speeds
questions.explanation: A robot parked for an hour has drifted by nothing. A number on a screen saying forty metres since the last fix turns a mysterious failure into an obvious one.

questions.question: Why must the test path differ from the calibration path?
options: Testing on the path you fitted the parameters to only confirms the fitting, not the parameters
To exercise more of the workspace
Because calibration paths are shorter
It does not need to differ if the calibration was careful
questions.explanation: The wheel base row is the proof: it is invisible on a straight line and costs a metre with turns. A calibration and a test that both drive straight will agree with each other and with nothing else.
